claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy with low platinum-group-metal content.
A 2–3 nm CeO2 layer can be deposited on the catalyst by ALD at approximately 200°C.
The ALD treatment produces a conformal CeO2 nanocoating on the underlying catalyst.
The CeO2 nanocoating acts as an oxygen-storage layer.
The CeO2 nanocoating acts as a physical barrier that stabilizes underlying active metal sites.
The CeO2 overcoat regulates local oxygen chemical potential through reversible redox cycling.
CeO2 redox cycling buffers the active sites against sudden variations in oxygen concentration.
The oxygen-buffering action inhibits sintering of active metal clusters.
The oxygen-buffering action inhibits phase segregation of active metal clusters.
The physical barrier prevents deleterious interactions between the active catalyst and H2O or NO.
The CeO2 overcoat preserves intrinsic catalytic activity under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The CeO2-coated catalyst will exhibit higher catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst during transient and low-temperature operation.
The CeO2-coated catalyst will exhibit more stable catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst.
The CeO2-coated catalyst will resist thermal-aging degradation better than the untreated catalyst.
The CeO2-coated catalyst will resist degradation associated with extended mileage better than the untreated catalyst.
An imprecisely controlled CeO2 layer may impose diffusion limitations and reduce intrinsic activity.
The optimal CeO2 overcoat thickness and its long-term stability under cyclic heating and redox conditions are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires improved performance relative to the untreated catalyst, but the falsification threshold is framed as retaining 90% of the coated catalyst's own initial activity 'relative to the untreated baseline.' This ambiguous criterion could be satisfied even if the coated catalyst performs worse than the untreated control, so it does not decisively test the stated relative-improvement claim.
